intro: Compare the surfaces around the figure. Ridges catch the light, gray values model a face, spray leaves a haze, and collage sets papers against one another.
alt: The same glasses-and-bun character in thick marine paint, gray modeling, a purple-green stencil and textured paper collage.

variants.name: palette knife painting
variants.look: Blunt raised ridges register where a palette knife pressed or dragged paint.
variants.history: Modern oil painters including Gustave Courbet used palette knives to spread paint broadly in expressive passages.
variants.when: Show the roughness of stone, fabric or a city wall with actual raised marks.
variants.why: A knife deposits broad dense paint while leaving the edges of individual strokes readable.

variants.name: grisaille
variants.look: Neutral grays make the face and clothing read as modeled relief.
variants.history: European painters used grisaille for independent works, underpainting and painted simulations of sculpture.
variants.when: Study volume or design an image to read in black and white.
variants.why: Restricting the palette puts emphasis on how one value moves into another.

variants.name: spray paint
variants.look: Violet and lime collect in stencil shapes with an aerosol halo.
variants.history: Twentieth-century artists used aerosol paint for both direct painting and stencils. Street artists used it for marks that could be made quickly on walls.
variants.when: Make a bold wall piece that can be read across a street.
variants.why: Spray turns a gesture into a broad mark and a stencil gives the edges greater control.

variants.name: mixed media
variants.look: Paper, fabric and painted marks keep their different edges and textures.
variants.history: Collage expanded the range of materials painters used in the early 20th century. Works by Picasso and Braque added papers and other fragments to painted surfaces.
variants.when: Combine documents, patterns and drawing marks in one scene.
variants.why: Each material brings its own texture and associations into the composition.

prompt: Create one square atlas comparison plate, precisely four independently composed equally sized artwork squares in full-bleed 2x2 grid, hard splits on both midlines, no margin nor gutter. Show the figure with her coffee during a pause at a tall window. The light on her face should have the same origin. Use the attached illustration only as subject character reference. 30-year-old attractive ash-blonde woman with tidy low bun, black rectangular eyeglasses clearly visible in every panel, tailored charcoal knee-length business dress under fitted blazer, signature white coffee mug with small four-color windowpane mark and plain blue lanyard with a blank badge. Never reproduce the card border or typography. The artwork techniques differ dramatically. Put nothing that crosses the splits. No letters, words, numerals or panel labels anywhere. TOP LEFT: palette knife oil painting, chunky blunt impasto ridges in marine blue and golden yellow. TOP RIGHT: grisaille, brush-painted sculpture illusion in only neutral grays and very carefully modeled light and shade. BOTTOM LEFT: spray paint stencil portrait on concrete, high contrast violet and lime street mural with spray edges and overspray flecks. BOTTOM RIGHT: mixed media, collage from torn patterned paper cutouts and ink outlines with fabric scraps and acrylic in red and teal.
